passage:
Last year Pallavi, then a third-year, wanted to be the helpful mentor for Aparna. Whenever Aparna got stuck, Pallavi typed the solution. Aparna nodded, thanked her, and came back the next day with the next problem. By the exams she could not write a loop alone.

This year, as a final-year student, Pallavi met a new junior, Naveen, and began differently. "What do you actually want?" she asked. "A first internship," he said. So instead of describing her own path, she looked at what internships asked for.

She broke "learn programming" down week by week: one concept, one exercise, one small program. Every Saturday they went over Naveen's work together, and Pallavi asked "what would you try?" before she said anything.

One Saturday Naveen asked about machine learning. Pallavi laughed. "I don't know it well enough to advise you. But a senior in that area is in the lab on Mondays. I'll introduce you." Naveen looked relieved that she had said it plainly.

qa.q: What did Naveen say he wanted?
qa.a: Naveen said he wanted a first internship.

qa.q: How did Pallavi's mentoring of Naveen differ from her earlier mentoring of Aparna, and what were the results?
qa.a: With Aparna she typed every solution, so Aparna could not write a loop alone, while with Naveen she asked what he wanted, set small weekly steps and asked what he would try first.

qa.q: What was Naveen feeling when Pallavi said she did not know machine learning well enough?
qa.a: Relief and trust, since she said it plainly and offered a real introduction.

qa.q: What could Pallavi do when Naveen is stuck next week?
qa.a: Pallavi could ask what he has tried and give a hint rather than the whole answer.

grounding: Four approaches to mentoring a junior: starting with their goal, small weekly steps, solving everything for them, and referring on when out of depth.
